slides.title: Hi, I’m Samarth
slides.body:
Product designer at Blink UX, an Mphasis company, in Austin. Five-plus years at Paytm, MakeMyTrip, Airtel Payments Bank and a few small teams.

A designer who's dream once started as a developer; and life (and AI) has got me full circle doing both now.

slides.title: Voyage
slides.lede: The design system behind $100M+ in enterprise deals

slides.title: Great work that vanished the day it shipped
slides.body:
Mphasis pre-sales wins deals from $1M to $100M by building demos of what a client’s product could look like.

A designer built ten screens for a pitch, then the work sat in someone’s Outlook. Two weeks later another designer rebuilt it from scratch.

visual.html: No shared language, no reusable components, no institutional memory. Just repeated effort, dressed up as bespoke work.

slides.title: Two to three months as a researcher, not a designer
slides.body:
Sole designer, end to end. Before opening Figma I interviewed the designers doing the work, the developers building the prototypes and the salespeople pitching them.

All of it went into one “God Document”, validated back with the people I’d interviewed.

visual.html:
The “God Document”

Five to ten years of pre-sales work, synthesised before a single screen was built

Client typesFinancial services, logistics, insurance: every account this team pitched
Solutions positionedWhat was proposed, to whom, and why it was chosen
Design patterns usedRecurring screens rebuilt from zero by a different designer, every time
What it revealedDifferent clients, same underlying patterns, rebuilt from scratch every time.

slides.title: Fifteen systems in, one backbone out
slides.body:
A week with Mphasis marketing on the real brand guidelines. Then two to three weeks studying fifteen design systems; four had kits deep enough to borrow from.

I themed a concept screen on each in Mphasis colours. Marketing picked Carbon’s depth and documentation as the backbone.

visual.html:
15Lightning, Manhattan, Material, Apple HIG, Uber, Ant, IBM Carbon and more
4Material · Carbon · Lightning · Uber, themed in Mphasis colours
1Carbon’s structure as the backbone

slides.title: Three to four months building before a single live deal
slides.body:
On a team that measured itself in weekly deal velocity, every week spent on the system made our output look slower by the old metric.

I made that bet anyway. One-off screens were the problem; building more of them faster wasn’t a fix, it was more of the disease.

stats: documented: spacing, type hierarchy, usage for every component

slides.title: Adopted, not just built
slides.body: I took it back to the designers I’d interviewed and spent one to two months refining it against their feedback. Then a new version roughly every two months, driven by wherever teams hit friction.

visual.html:
v1Foundation

UI kit, core components, brand colours

v2+ Data viz

Tables, charts and graphs. Teams enter values instead of drawing by hand

v3+ White-label

One-click reskin across 20+ client brands

v4+ Refinements

slides.title: What used to be a rebuild became a toggle
slides.body:
Sales wanted demos themed to the client being pitched, not a generic Mphasis screen.

So I built variable theme sets: one switch reskins colour, type and components for any of 20+ client brands.

Try the toggle. A simplified code demo with neutral themes, not client branding.

slides.title: Not everyone designs in Figma anymore
slides.body:
I researched how designers here work today: Claude (Code, Design, the chat), GPT and other LLMs, BMAD, Figma and Figma agents.

So the next step was a system that guides those tools, with humans and AI agents creating UX and maintaining it together.

visual.html:
Claude CodeClaude DesignClaude chatGPTOther LLMsBMADFigmaFigma agents
Voyagetokens · principles · components · docs

slides.title: How humans and AI co-create UI
slides.body: Reuse first. New components only when there’s a real gap, and a person signs off at every gate.

visual.html:
01 · IntentPerson describes the need and contextAI pulls the relevant principles, tokens and components
02 · ReuseReuses or extends the existing systemNo new components needed, design createdDraft UX screen
03 · Create only if a gap existsProposes a component only for a real gapPerson approves the needScope: which line of business, which kitCode, states, examples and testsDraft component
04 · ReviewCode quality and UX acceptanceAutomated accessibility, responsive and regression checksFinal component + screen
05 · GrowApproved components go back into the shared systemFinal check before it ships to everyone
HumanAIOutput

slides.title: Users started leaving

visual.html:
For years

Paytm was the default way to send money.

Then

Google Pay let you chat while paying.

So

People were moving to UPI. Paytm had to answer.

slides.title: Go further than the basics
slides.body: Chat plus payments was only where we started. UPI was the starting point, not the whole idea.

visual.html:
Google Pay hadChat while you pay
We addedGroup chats
We addedBill splitting
We addedGroup savings pools
The foundation forInvesting conversations

slides.title: Send button is a compliance conversation
slides.body:
Paytm had never had chat: no bubble style, no message states. We were defining primitives in about the most regulated consumer space in India.

Every component went into Paytm’s core design system and needed legal, business and management sign-off.

visual.html:
Dinner was great! How much do I owe?
₹640 each 🍕Read ✓✓
Payment received₹640Paid instantly · 2 sec
Thanks!❤️Delivered ✓✓
See you FridaySent ✓

Sent, delivered, read and reacted-to: each state got its own tested treatment. Illustration recreated in code for this deck.

slides.title: Payment cards had to feel like chat, and pass compliance
slides.body: Payment cards in chat were a new direction for payments, with more traceability. They also had to cover every use case.

slides.title: One sticker, many stickers, and what shows while loading
slides.body: Stickers were our stand-out feature: upload a transparent GIF, get an animated sticker. I worked through rendering and every state with developers.

slides.title: PODS wasn’t built for chat
slides.body:
PODS, Paytm’s design system, was very new back then.

I added elements that fit it and carried the chat team’s vision, each with states, animations, size guidance and interaction guides. They stayed in the system as a new component category.

slides.title: People open the app to pay, not to chat
slides.body:
Other apps made you start a chat, then pay. Our statistics and interviews showed the reverse.

So paying someone connects to a chat or starts one. Within 2–3 months, the market was adapting too.

slides.title: Designing stickers with the launch in mind
slides.body:
I worked with business and marketing to see how they planned to advertise stickers, and we made custom stickers for launch.

Product screenshots, with marketing’s input, went into the collateral. That bridged a major gap in the team.

slides.title:
Trust is the whole game
in payments
slides.body: We designed every message state in real depth. I still think that care is why it felt trustworthy, fast.

slides.title: The business disappeared in about three weeks
slides.body:
Insider’s entire business was offline events: ticketing and in-person shows. Then COVID happened.

We had six months of runway and no product. The mandate was simple to say and hard to do: build something people would pay for, fast, with no idea yet what that was.

stats: for the core business to vanish
of runway to find a new one

slides.title: Clubhouse and Google Meet each solved half of it
slides.body:
Clubhouse had the intimacy of audio-first rooms. Meet had scheduled, hosted structure. I compared them on five things.

Then user interviews and a value stream: what someone gets done when they come back a second time. I argued it out with the business until both lined up.

visual.html:
ClubhouseGoogle Meet
Audio vs videoLive audio roomsVideo conferencing
ExclusivityInvitation-only launchCorporate, closed use
CommunityRooms by shared interestCollaborative meetings
ModerationHost-controlled roomsAdmin controls
MonetisationCreator monetisationNone native
Insider VibesChat, audio and video in one: room-based communities with moderation and experience levels

slides.title: Three roles, three products inside one
slides.body: Most platforms design for participants and bolt on tooling for everyone else. We designed all three properly, because a community with weak moderation isn’t a community for long.

visual.html:
AdminCreate rooms, manage users, oversee content, set rules
ModeratorsSupport admins, monitor discussions, de-escalate conflict, report upward
ParticipantsParticipate, follow rules, build the community, personalise their profile

slides.title: A plug-and-play design system on a six-month runway
slides.body:
Every instinct said ship the fastest version and fix it later. I built the system flexible down to fonts, colours and components, knowing it would slow the first weeks.

Midway, engineering moved the stack from Angular to React. The interface barely felt it.

visual.html:
SlowerFirst few weeks

Building tokens and components before screens

Paid offAngular → React

Full stack rebuild midway, and the UI barely moved

slides.title: The design system underneath all of it
slides.body: Three fully designed roles, a joining flow that showed upfront what the platform could see and hear, and camera and mic controls front and centre. The system was translated into React components with the dev team so it could scale past v1 without a redesign.

slides.title: The expanding panel
slides.body: The bottom half is information-dense and some people want to live in it. Instead of a separate view, the top half shrinks as you scroll so the bottom can breathe. Removes a whole navigation step.

slides.title: Polls that interrupt just enough
slides.body: A bottom sheet on mobile, a small box top-right on desktop, animated in Protopie and Rive. Enough to answer, not enough to lose your place in the conversation.

slides.title: The room was worth coming back to
slides.body: The first number kept the company alive. The second is the one I care about: 62% coming back means the room itself was worth it, not just the novelty.

Note from future Samarth

I set up CleverTap A/B tests and moved teams before seeing the results. Now I hand off a test with an owner and a date to check back. I’d also push harder to be in the room for stack decisions like Angular to React.
